transcript.content:
Honestly I'd be surprised if the Moon can be seen right now, but give me your honest estimate anyway.

I'm in Cairo, Egypt at 2026-06-15 14:22 EEST (UTC+0300) (2026-06-15T11:22:00Z in UTC), at latitude 30.0444 degrees and longitude 31.2357 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 69.598 degrees and its azimuth is 255.926 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 75.499 degrees and its azimuth is 265.432 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 0.35 percent illuminated, 6.757 degrees from the Sun, and 351259.2 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

To be completely honest: **No, you will not be able to see it.**

Even though your app correctly shows that the Moon is physically above the horizon, there are three specific astronomical and physiological reasons why it will be invisible to your naked eye in these conditions:

### 1. The "Daylight Washout" Effect
The Sun is currently at an altitude of nearly 70 degrees. At this angle, the atmosphere is scattering a massive amount of sunlight (Rayleigh scattering), creating a very high level of ambient sky brightness. For an object to be visible during the day, it needs to have a high **contrast** against the blue of the sky. 

### 2. The Phase (0.35% Illumination)
This is the biggest hurdle. At 0.35% illumination, the Moon is in its "New Moon" phase. Only a tiny sliver—barely a microscopic crescent—is reflecting sunlight. Because the Moon is so close to the Sun (only 6.7 degrees away), the side of the Moon that *is* illuminated is facing almost directly toward the Sun. 

From your perspective on Earth, you are looking at the "dark side" of the Moon. Even if the sky were pitch black, you would struggle to see it; in bright daylight, that tiny sliver of light is completely overwhelmed by the surrounding glare.

### 3. The Proximity to the Sun
Because the Moon is only 6.7 degrees away from the Sun, it is sitting in the brightest part of the sky. The "glare" from the Sun's position creates a visual "blind spot." Even if there were a larger crescent, it would be lost in the solar glare, much like trying to see a firefly hovering right next to a high-powered stadium floodlight.

### The Verdict
If you were to look toward the azimuth of 265° (roughly West-Southwest), you would see a very bright, washed-out sky. You might see some high-altitude clouds or haze, but the Moon will be effectively invisible.

**How you could see it:**
If you had a pair of **high-powered binoculars** or a **telescope**, you might be able to spot it because the optics would help isolate the Moon's position from the surrounding sky brightness. But with unaided eyesight? It’s a "no."
